 Barbados PM wants Caribbean to remain a zone of peace 







UNITED NATIONS (CMC) – Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley on Thursday called for the Caribbean region to remain a zone of peace and that there should be no acceptance of the region “becoming a theatre for confrontation or for the unilateral and unjustified use of force”.

In an address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), Mottley said that it is also necessary for political leaders in the Caribbean to play a pivotal role in ensuring that the region remains peaceful and progressive.

She said that in the French-speaking Caribbean Community (Caricom) country of Haiti, where criminal gangs are seeking to overthrow the government following the assassination of President Jovenel Moise in 2021, the security crisis continues to retard political renewal and economic recovery.

“Still, preparations for a return to constitutional government are moving forward, even with great difficulty. But those efforts cannot succeed unless security improves, particularly in the areas containing more than half of Haiti’s electorate,” she argued.

She said as a result, Barbados supports the full deployment that has been long-promised and the renewal of the mandate of the 5,500 Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multinational security mission authorised by the United Nations Security Council to combat armed gangs in Haiti.

“Let me remind you that it was in 2022 that this recent, more heightened state of insecurity began with the fuel riots. Enough is enough. At the same time, we thank all member states who have contributed in whatever way to helping Haiti find its path,” she said.

Mottley said that this includes the three-member Caricom Eminent Persons Group (EPG), chaired by the former St Lucia prime minister Dr Kenny Anthony and including Bruce Golding and Perry Christie, the former prime ministers of Jamaica and The Bahamas respectively.

She said that EPG has been helping to build consensus in Haiti and maintain engagement with key international partners.

Mottley said that the region is also “deeply concerned” by the worsening humanitarian pressures facing the people of Cuba as the United States, which has in place a decades-old trade and economic embargo against Havana, has in recent months stepped up its programme of seeking to remove the government on the island.

The aggressive strategy, led by the Donald Trump administration, has pushed the island into an unprecedented humanitarian and economic crisis, and following Washington’s removal of the Nicolás Maduro government in Venezuela, it has completely halted Venezuelan oil shipments to Cuba, cutting off the island’s primary energy lifeline.

“Too many people are suffering. Restrictions on trade, finance and access to fuel are intensifying hardship not only for Cuban citizens, but also for all others who study and live there,” Mottley said, adding that Barbados has, each year, opposed the use of the embargo and other unilateral coercive measures against Cuba.

“As always, we call for constructive engagement. This must be grounded in dialogue, sovereign equality and respect for international law. “

Mottley said that Barbados was also extending its continued solidarity to the people of Venezuela as they recover from the devastating double earthquakes in June and that Bridgetown remains committed to supporting the South American country’s longer-term recovery.

“A stable, sovereign, peaceful and democratic Venezuela is vital to the security and prosperity of the wider Caribbean. In this regard, I take this opportunity to reiterate Barbados’ steadfast support to its sister Caricom country of Guyana as it seeks to bring a peaceful resolution, through the International Court of Justice, to the long- outstanding controversy with Venezuela.

“This is in the interest of the people of Guyana, Venezuela and the people of the wider Caribbean,” Mottley said, adding “the Caribbean must remain a Zone of Peace.”

In her address, Mottley said that on March 25 this year, the United Nations adopted a “historic resolution” where the overwhelming majority of states acknowledged the truth that the trafficking of enslaved African and Racialised Chattel Enslavement of Africans was the gravest crime against humanity.

“Yes, we in Barbados painfully know this reality. Regrettably, we still carry the scars. I have reminded us that it was my country that passed the first Slave Code in 1661. Others followed, including the infamous Code Noir of 1685. It was only repealed this year; hence the wounds are still raw,” said Mottley.

She said Barbados accepts the moral responsibility of removing the cross of slavery with its horrific consequences, adding, “We must effect healing through reparatory justice. It is the right thing to do.”

She said in July, Caribbean leaders approved the revised Caricom Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, telling the global community “for the Caribbean, for Africa and for all of those countries concerned, the honest engagement must begin.

“We do not ask for reparations without accepting responsibility for our own self-repair, which we have undertaken for decades. I want to be very clear about this Mr President. Let there be no doubt. The mindset that established, justified and sustained slavery is the same mindset that sustains the iniquities and inequities within the power structures of this very institution and within the international financial architecture. The same mindset that caused a global map to remain grossly inaccurate for centuries,” she said.

news.title: EU to Condemn War in Ukraine at G20 Even if Putin Attends
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The European Union said on Thursday that it would continue to condemn Russia's war in Ukraine at the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December.It said that it would do this regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin attends after being invited by this year's hosting country, the United States. The Kremlin has said that Putin would "consider" Washington's invitation.The Russian leader did not attend the G20 summit in 2023 in New Delhi, India and the 2022 summit on the Indonesian island of Bali despite being formally invited by the hosting countries.Also on Thursday, eight people were killed in a wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.What did the EU say about Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit?The EU said it would continue calling for an end to the war in Ukraine."Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion [of Ukraine] and to call for it to end," EU spokesman Olof Gill said."What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."Gill said that Russia remained a member of the G20 group and that it had "the right to participate" in its meetings.Both the European Union itself and three of its individual member states — France, Germany, and Italy — are members of the G20 group.What is the US position on Putin's attendance at the G20?Ukraine's allies — including G20 members France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and Canada — have called for Russia's exclusion from the group since Moscow launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was inviting Putin after his meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York."We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with [US President Donald Trump], but with other world leaders," Rubio said on Wednesday. "We hope that's an invitation he'll accept."Putin's last visit to the United States was to attend a summit meeting with Trump in Anchorage, Alaska in August 15, 2025, also marking his first visit to a Western country since the start of the war in Ukraine.Russian strikes kill 8 in Kharkiv, KyivAt least six agricultural workers were killed and 12 others were wounded in a strike on the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.The regional prosecutor's office published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse following the attack.Ukrainian authorities said that the warehouse had been hit by a small-sized cruise missile of the "Banderol" type.Meanwhile, at least two people were killed across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, Prime Minsiter Serhiy Koretsky said.Strikes were also recorded in and around the southwestern port city of Odesa, with officials reporting they sparked a fire at a shopping mall.Read: Poland Says Starlink Station Fire 'Act of Sabotage'Click here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News

news.title: Allies unite behind Saudi Arabia as Houthis step up attacks
news.text:
RIYADH/CAIRO: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan will hold an urgent, high-level meeting under a joint defence pact to discuss ways to support the kingdom amid attacks by ​Yemen’s Houthis, while Tehran sought to distance itself from the rapid advance of its Houthi allies.

The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and repeatedly fired ‌into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

The Houthis said they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets on Thursday, while authorities in Saudi Arabia said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

Saudi Arabia earlier had issued emergency alerts for areas including the holy city of Makkah, Jeddah and Yanbu, the main Saudi Red ​Sea oil port.

Saudi Arabia’s top religious authority called on soldiers in the kingdom to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group is ousted from power, ​a statement posted on the Saudi state news agency said.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Makkah Joint ⁠Defence Agreement, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement. They condemned the attacks targeting Makkah and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself, the statement said.

“The ministers also discussed arrangements for ​holding an urgent meeting of the chiefs of staff of the three countries to discuss ways to support Saudi Arabia under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which stipulates that an attack against any one of the ​parties constitutes an attack against all parties,” the statement said.

The meeting was announced shortly after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sought to distance Iran from the Houthis in an American television interview on Thursday.

“The Houthis are responsible for their own actions,” Pezeshkian told the Fox News program “Special Report with Bret Baier” a day after he appeared before the UN General Assembly in New York.

The Pezeshkian interview and speech took place amid a pause in fighting between the US and Iran and a brief attempt ​at diplomacy in New York, with Qatar serving as intermediary between the warring parties.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the United States via intermediaries under ​which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened if Tehran’s conditions were met.

Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen ‌funds and ⁠waive its oil sanctions, he said.

“The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day,” Araqchi said, adding that talks with the United States on other issues, including Iran’s nuclear issue, would then start.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to its peace proposals.

The war, which US President Donald Trump launched alongside Israel in February, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global energy supplies, pushing up oil prices.

While the US and Iran have largely stood down from direct combat, Iranian allies are engaged in the region with Hezbollah confronting Israel in Lebanon and the Houthis advancing in Yemen.

Iran and its allies have ​significantly pressured oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ​ally.

The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at ⁠the mouth of the Red Sea while Iran has effectively limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of the world’s oil exports before the start of the war. An attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq also temporarily knocked Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline out of service.

Security experts have debated exactly ​how much Iran directly influences the Houthis, a Shia movement that evolved from a local insurgency into a powerful armed group controlling much of ​northern Yemen.

However, Yemeni government, Iranian ⁠and regional sources have said the Houthis’ advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast was carried out with direct guidance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

With the US-Israeli war against Iran largely stalemated for months on the battlefield, Washington has announced a shift in tactics to extend the reach of its financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms, a practice known as “secondary sanctions”.

Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the UAE ⁠and Oman on ​Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of a shift in US policy to target companies in ​third countries that do business with Iran.

A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran’s isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the country, which is already facing a US blockade of its ports at sea.

“We are living in an open-air prison,” a retired teacher ​in Tehran told Reuters by text message on condition her name not be used.

news.title: Socialist candidate for Congress reveals she got arrested protesting Netanyahu at the United Nations
news.text:
As Benjamin Netanyahu prepared to take the podium inside the United Nations, a Democratic congressional candidate was being led away in handcuffs outside. 

Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th Congressional District, was among at least 30 people arrested Thursday during a protest against the Israeli prime minister’s appearance at the UN General Assembly. 

The demonstration, organized by Jewish Voice for Peace amongst other progressive organizations, saw protesters block a roadway near the UN headquarters.

Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and New York City Council member Chi Ossé were also detained as well as whistle blower Chelsea Manning.

In an extraordinary first-person account to The Guardian, Chevalier confirmed her arrest outside the UN and framed the demonstration as an act of political resistance towards funding Israel through US taxpayer money.

'As the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional district, I refuse to allow a war criminal to roam the streets of our city unchallenged. I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children with American taxpayer dollars.'

She continued, 'That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.'

In her account, she accused Netanyahu and the Israeli government of responsibility for devastating conditions in Gaza using the contentious term 'genocide' and condemned US military support for Israel, additionally blaming the US for 'shielding Netanyahu from persecution.' 

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity connected to the Gaza conflict. Netanyahu and Israeli officials have rejected the allegations of genocide and says its military campaign is aimed at Hamas.

The confrontation outside the UN also comes against the backdrop of a fierce political dispute over whether American officials could or should act on that warrant.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has previously said he would seek to enforce the warrant against Netanyahu if legally empowered to do so, although the issue of municipal authority has remained disputed. However, President Donald Trump has declared that Netanyahu will not be arrested on US soil.

Chevalier also attacked what she described as the 'establishment' of both major American parties for continuing to support Israel.

That language goes straight to the heart of the political insurgency that carried her to the Democratic nomination.

A self-described Democratic Socialist and longtime pro-Palestinian activist, Chevalier stunned New York’s Democratic establishment in June when she defeated five-term incumbent Adriano Espaillat in the Democratic primary for the heavily Democratic 13th District.

She has campaigned on Democratic Socialist themes, opposition to US military intervention and a fundamental redistribution of government priorities toward housing, healthcare and other domestic programs. Her campaign describes her as a community organizer with more than a decade of activism in Upper Manhattan and the Bronx.

Her political ascent has already unsettled sections of the Democratic establishment.

The Washington Post reported before her primary victory that Republicans were seeking to use her record and controversial past comments to portray her as emblematic of the party’s leftward shift. 

Her past, now-deleted, social media posts included rants about interracial relationships.

She wrote that black and Arab men who are with white women 'fetishize ugly colonizer women.'

She also previously called for 'abolishing the border', and when pressed over that view, she responded: 'Yes literally abolish the border, all deportation is wrong.'

Avila Chevalier also sparked backlash for joking about wiping her dirty hands on the American flag, and she has previously described the US as a 'disgrace.' 

The arrest gives Avila Chevalier an extraordinary new chapter in a congressional campaign that has already become a symbol of the Democratic Party’s increasingly bitter ideological struggle between its progressive left and its more established political wing.

As Netanyahu prepared to defend Israel’s conduct before the General Assembly, demonstrators outside were chanting against the war and demanding an end to US support for Israel. 

Protesters, however, described the conflict as an issue of American responsibility because US taxpayer money supports Israel.

For Avila Chevalier, the contrast was precisely the point. She has argued that Washington spends enormous sums supporting overseas military operations while communities in her own district struggle with poverty, housing insecurity and cuts to public assistance. 

'Our enemy is a system where billionaires get rich from stoking hatred and war while our own communities go without', said Avila Chevalier's account.

In her account of the protest, she invoked Martin Luther King Jr’s opposition to excessive military spending and presented her campaign as a challenge to what she calls the American 'insatiable war machine.' 

Avila Chevalier has ensured that her campaign is no longer merely part of the ideological battle consuming New York Democrats.

As of now Mamdani has not weighed in on the arrest of Chevalier, whom he has endorsed.
news.summary: New York congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier was arrested while protesting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's UN speech on Thursday.
news.author: Editor,Sophia Baum

news.title: China’s Xi shares a rare laugh on White House tour at Trump’s Biden autopen joke
news.text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping broke into rare laughter as his US counterpart Donald Trump showed him a framed “autopen” displayed in place of the former American leader Joe Biden’s portrait during a White House tour.
The viral moment stood out against the Chinese leader’s otherwise restrained demeanour during his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade.
A video released by the White House on social media showed Trump taking Xi along the White House colonnade on Thursday before stopping at the “Presidential Walk of Fame”, where portraits and plaques honour US presidents.
“This is the autopen ... it’s Biden,” Trump said, pointing to the image. Xi laughed audibly, while several people accompanying the two leaders also appeared to join in.
While parts of Trump’s remarks were difficult to make out in the video, he appeared to be referring sarcastically to Biden’s use of the autopen, a recurring target of the US president’s criticism of his predecessor.

The moment offered a striking contrast with Xi’s generally composed public demeanour during the state visit which is occurring against a backdrop of bilateral tensions surrounding technology and rare earths.
At Wednesday’s welcome ceremony, Xi showed little reaction when a jet taking part in a military flyover produced a thunderous roar as the US national anthem was being played. Trump, standing nearby, appeared startled by the noise and briefly grimaced.
After Xi laughed at the autopen joke, Trump gave the Chinese president a friendly pat on the shoulder as they continued the tour.
Trump is known for using expansive gestures and physical contact when meeting foreign leaders. During his previous encounters with Xi, however, the Chinese president has generally maintained a more formal posture.
In Trump’s visit to China in May, Xi appeared to deny Trump his trademark tug of war – style handshake, holding firm as the US president tried to draw him closer.
Thursday’s video quickly drew attention on social media. “I have never heard Xi laughing so genuinely with Trump about Biden’s autopen portrait,” one post said. “Quite a moment,” another commenter wrote.
The image of an autopen has occupied the place of Joe Biden’s portrait in Trump’s “Presidential Walk of Fame” since September 2025.
Trump has routinely denigrated his predecessor, refusing to acknowledge his 2020 election loss to Biden and repeatedly peddling the claim that the result was rigged by voter fraud.
He has also repeatedly accused Biden of relying on aides and the autopen to sign official documents by the end of his term in office, allegations that Biden’s administration has disputed.

A separate video shared by White House staff also showed Trump stopping in front of a framed photograph from his meeting with Xi in Beijing in May.
Trump pointed at the photograph and asked, “Who is this? I don’t recognise him.”
Xi turned towards members of his delegation and appeared to give another brief laugh.
US-China relations plummeted to new lows during Biden’s term as a sequence of flashpoints unravelled diplomatic ties.
Sharp recriminations over the origins of Covid-19 were compounded by a major cross-strait crisis triggered by then-US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s Taiwan visit in 2022.
Other tensions involved the 2023 “spy balloon” saga and an array of tech-containment measures targeting China’s semiconductor and investment landscapes.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

After Biden took office in January 2021, he held three formal in-person meetings with Xi, all on the sidelines of multilateral meetings including the G20. No state visits were exchanged between Washington and Beijing during the former US president’s tenure.
Xi’s last trip to the United States was in November 2023, when he travelled to San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and met then-president Biden.
Before that, Xi’s last state visit to Washington was in September 2015, when then-US vice-president Biden and his wife Jill Biden welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at the airport.

Chinese President Xi Jinping broke into rare laughter as his US counterpart Donald Trump showed him a framed “autopen” displayed in place of the former American leader Joe Biden’s portrait during a White House tour.
The viral moment stood out against the Chinese leader’s otherwise restrained demeanour during his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade.

news.title: Chinese president says he had frank, in-depth talks with Donald Trump
news.text:
BEIJING, September 25. /TASS/. Chinese President Xi Jinping said he had held a frank and comprehensive exchange of opinions with his US counterpart Donald Trump.

"Today, President Trump and I had a sincere and in-depth exchange of views," the Chinese leader said during a state dinner at the White House.

He went on to say that their talks have given new meaning to the relations of strategic stability between the two nations.

"This [the meeting] infused new substance into the constructive China-US relations, based on strategic stability, and defined the new strategic guidelines for the China-US ties," Xi Jinping added.

news.title: Netanyahu Calls Gaza Genocide Claims ‘Century’s Biggest Lie’
news.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu has dismissed accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza as “the biggest lie of the century,” delivering a combative speech at the United Nations after scores of delegates walked out when he took the stage.

The Israeli prime minister faced a mixture of applause, boos and jeers as he made his way to the podium in New York. Large numbers of representatives stood up and left the chamber.

By the time Netanyahu began speaking, much of the visible seating area was empty. Members of the Israeli delegation, however, remained on their feet, applauding their prime minister.

The disruption led General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman to call for order several times.

Netanyahu responded by condemning those who had left the hall, including representatives from Spain, Ireland, Egypt and Syria.

“If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t left this hall, please do so now,” he said.

The walkout followed a call from the Palestinian Mission to the UN, which had encouraged member states to bring as many staff members as possible into the chamber and leave together when Netanyahu was introduced.

The Palestinian message said the coordinated protest would show that countries refused to be “complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation”.

Israel rejects accusations of genocide and war crimes, while also disputing claims that its presence in Palestinian territory is unlawful.

Addressing an overwhelmingly critical international audience, Netanyahu offered an uncompromising defence of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and its broader regional confrontation with Iran.

He described the decision to strike Iran as one of the easiest choices he had made, arguing that Israel’s military actions were also safeguarding the countries whose representatives had just departed the chamber.

“In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said. “In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes.”

With his voice growing more emphatic, Netanyahu repeated that attacking Iran “was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make”.

He also used the UN speech to confront claims that Israel’s conduct in Gaza constitutes genocide.

“Allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza are not only false but ‘the biggest lie of the century’,” he declared.

The prime minister highlighted what he called Israel’s efforts to protect civilians and deliver aid, while accusing its critics of offering a misleading portrayal of the conflict.

His address came after a week of speeches at the UN in which numerous world leaders had condemned Israel’s conduct in Gaza and called for an end to the conflict.

The war began after Hamas-led militants attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, killing around 1,200 people and abducting 251 others.

At least 73,922 Palestinians have subsequently been killed in Israel’s offensive, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government. International organisations have generally regarded the ministry’s casualty figures as credible, although the figures do not distinguish between civilians and combatants in the overall toll.

A ceasefire agreed between Israel and Hamas last October brought an end to the heaviest fighting and resulted in the release of the remaining hostages, but subsequent negotiations have stalled.

Israel still controls most of Gaza and continues to conduct strikes near military-held areas, while Hamas has not disarmed or surrendered control of the territory.

Netanyahu also used the UN platform to defend Israel against criticism over violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

He dismissed what he described as exaggerated coverage of the issue, while making clear he did not approve of attacks against Palestinians.

‘What [the media] cover is a handful of young juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who go or throw stones, who chop down olive trees,’ Netanyahu said.

‘I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism.’

The comments come amid international criticism of Israeli settlement expansion and settler violence in the West Bank.

The Prime Minister also turned his attention to Britain and France, accusing both countries of hypocrisy over allegations that Israel is pursuing a colonial project.

‘They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism.

‘And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term.’

He also took aim at New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has repeatedly described Netanyahu as a ‘war criminal’ and has called for his arrest.

‘Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York,’ Netanyahu said. ‘You falsely, repeatedly accuse Israel of genocide.’

Mr Mamdani has acknowledged that New York City does not have the authority to enforce an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, but has urged the US federal authorities to act.

Netanyahu’s appearance came during an increasingly tense period in relations between Israel and parts of the international community, with criticism of its Gaza campaign intensifying.

Before his speech, Netanyahu had promised to use his appearance at the General Assembly to defend Israel and confront what he described as misinformation about the country’s conduct.

He also invoked the October 7 attacks during his address, comparing the death toll to the September 11 attacks in the United States.

He held up a pager during the speech while recalling Israel’s 2024 attack on thousands of devices used by the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon.

The pager explosions killed 12 people, including two children, and wounded more than 3,000.

Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for taking action against Iran and vowed that Israel would continue its military campaign.

‘We will continue to win because we have no other choice.’

Netanyahu’s address followed a prerecorded speech by Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, who was unable to travel to New York after the United States denied visas to him and other senior Palestinian officials for a second consecutive year.

The 90-year-old Palestinian leader used his address to reject any suggestion that Palestinians would leave their homeland.

‘We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. And we will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf,’ Mr Abbas said.

He also challenged countries that continue to supply Israel with weapons.

‘How long will some countries continue to remain silent about Israel, or continue supplying it with weapons that it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the enormous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank,’ Abbas said. ‘What, then, is the international community waiting for before it acts to protect the Palestinian people?’

The confrontation inside the UN was mirrored by angry demonstrations on the streets of Manhattan, where protesters gathered ahead of Netanyahu’s appearance.

Among those detained by NYPD officers were Hollywood actresses Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder, who were taking part in a pro-Palestinian demonstration outside the UN.

The pair were seen wearing white T-shirts bearing the words ‘fund people not bombs’ as police moved in to clear First Avenue.

Comedian and actor Caleb Hearon was also detained, alongside a number of New York City council members, according to reports.

More than 100 people were arrested during the demonstrations, according to protest organisers, while images showed police officers detaining protesters in the street.

The protests were among several demonstrations held in New York during Netanyahu’s visit, with hundreds of people gathering outside the UN and chanting slogans calling for an end to the war.

news.title: Asian stocks weather bond storm, oil retreats slightly
news.text:
SYDNEY: Asian shares held their nerve on Friday as a relentless bond selloff pushed longer dated US yields ​to two-decade highs, raising borrowing costs worldwide and threatening lofty equity valuations.

The return of oil above $100 a barrel, with Brent crude ‌near $105, has revived inflation fears, bolstering bets on multiple Federal Reserve rate hikes after its first move in more than three years and putting the dollar on track for a 1% weekly gain.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is in Washington for talks with President Donald Trump, though beneath the fanfare there has been scant evidence of breakthroughs on ​thorny issues over AI, trade, Taiwan or the war with Iran.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was flat, with ​most markets including Chinese mainland, Taiwan and South Korea closed for a holiday.

Japan’s Nikkei rose 1%, while Australia’s resources-heavy ⁠shares fell 0.6%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index skidded 1%.

Risk assets are being squeezed by a dramatic selloff in global bonds, as inflation ​worries and fiscal strains push investors to demand ever-higher returns particularly on long-dated debt.

“The world’s bond markets are screaming, and ignoring it could prove ​very expensive,” said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.

“Once risk-free rates sit above 5% in the world’s largest economy, every asset on the planet has to justify its price against that. Equities, property, private credit, emerging market debt - nothing’s immune.”

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose 1 basis point to 5.1915%, having surged ​20 bps in just two days to a new 19-year peak of 5.2251%. That was the biggest two-day gain since April last year when ​Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs spooked markets.

Thirty-year US bond yields climbed 2 basis points to 5.4805%, having surged 16 bps over the past two days to hit ‌5.5016%, the ⁠highest since 2004. That lifted US mortgage rates to 7%, hamstringing the housing market.

Asian bonds extended the global selloff, with Japan’s 10-year government bond yields up 4 bps to 3.115%, the highest since 1996. Australia’s 10-year government bond yields also rose 4 bps to 5.408%.

Global hiking cycle reaches scandinavia

There was no respite at the short end of the Treasury curve either. Fed funds futures now imply a 71% chance of another rate hike next ​month, up from about 53% earlier ​this week, and more than ⁠90 basis points of tightening still to come this cycle, equivalent to almost four quarter-point hikes.

The US 2-year yields were steady at 4.9035%, having jumped 16 bps this week to hover near a two-year high.

The Fed’s ​return to rate hikes last week is rippling across global markets. As inflation pressures intensify, smaller central banks ​are shifting to a ⁠more hawkish stance, with Norway’s Norges Bank raising rates on Thursday and Sweden’s Riksbank signalling it was likely to follow suit by the year end.

Mexico’s Banxico held rates steady but dropped its previous guidance for a prolonged pause.

That is keeping the US dollar firm, having risen 1% this week to 101.25 ⁠against its ​major peers, about the highest since late July.

In the commodities market, Brent crude eased ​0.8% to $105.75 a barrel, after climbing 3% overnight as a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia revived fears of supply disruptions.

Markets are meanwhile clinging on to lingering hopes for a ​possible truce between the US and Iran, as the two countries are reportedly exploring a phased path to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

news.title: How Trump’s Attendance Is Affecting Football Games: The Unseen Impact
news.text:
Donald Trump’s planned appearance at Saturday’s high-profile college football matchup between Tennessee and Texas could directly affect how players and coaches communicate during the game.

The White House confirmed this week that the President will travel to Knoxville for the marquee SEC contest before attending The Presidents Cup on Sunday.

Texas coach Steve Sarkisian has now detailed the extensive security measures expected at Neyland Stadium, including a protocol that could temporarily cut off his team’s communications without warning.

Speaking on Wednesday, Sarkisian explained that communications are suspended whenever the President enters or exits the stadium, or moves between locations inside the venue.

“The one thing you have to be aware of when the President goes to any game is that any time he enters the stadium, leaves the stadium or changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication,” he said.

“They cut the coaches’ headsets and the coach-to-player communication. You have to have a plan for that if and when it happens, and you get no warning. The communication simply cuts out.

Sarkisian said a similar disruption occurred during last year’s national championship game between Indiana and Miami, when Trump was also in attendance.

“A good friend of mine is [Miami head coach] Mario Cristobal. When they played Indiana in last year’s national championship, they had that drive at the end of the game,” Sarkisian said.

“They had no communication because he was leaving before the game had finished. You get no warning; it just cuts out. You have to be prepared for it.”

This will not be Sarkisian’s first experience with the procedure. He encountered it in 2019 while serving as Alabama’s offensive coordinator, when Trump attended the Crimson Tide’s meeting with LSU in Tuscaloosa.

Since returning to the Oval Office, Trump has attended several major sporting occasions, including the World Cup final, the Ryder Cup and the US Open final.

Those appearances have brought heightened security operations, creating significant knock-on effects for the thousands of spectators inside and around each venue.

This summer, fans were still waiting outside Madison Square Garden when Game 3 of the NBA Finals began because of intensified security checks.

Similarly, Trump’s appearance at last year’s men’s US Open final delayed the match by 30 minutes and produced lengthy security queues for frustrated tennis fans.

Organizers would later apologize to fans for the delays, saying: ‘We understand the frustration of fans that were delayed in their entrance to Arthur Ashe Stadium. 

‘The added security protocols were put in place by the United States Secret Service. We took several steps to make this process as seamless as possible and educate our attendees on the potential delays in advance of their arrival.’

Meanwhile, it was revealed on Thursday that Trump is not expected to appear on ESPN’s College GameDay on Saturday, despite speculation that he could join the desk before Tennessee’s clash with Texas.

Rumors went into overdrive earlier this week after the White House confirmed that Trump will be in Knoxville to attend the SEC showdown at Neyland Stadium.

The game will kick off at 12pm ET – with ESPN’s College GameDay in town for the first ever regular season meeting between Texas and Tennessee.

Given Trump’s friendship with hosts Pat McAfee and Nick Saban, fans began speculating that the President could feature as a guest picker or join the broadcast.

However, sources have since told Front Office Sports that Trump is not anticipated to make an appearance on the iconic pregame show prior to kickoff on the day.

news.title: 'Pope Fever' Takes Hold as Pope Leo Visits France
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - France is gripped by "Pope fever." Since the 1905 French law on separating church and state, the country has embraced secular traditions. But over the next few days, the streets will tell a different story.From Friday, Pope Leo XIV will spend four days in France, visiting Paris, Lourdes and Metz. All his public events have been sold out for weeks. Organizers expect around 1 million people to fill the streets of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air mass at the Place de la Concorde."The pope is popular among both believers and nonbelievers," political scientist Olivier Roy told DW. He added that Leo XIV's conflict with US President Donald Trump in particular had lent him "a moral standing that extends far beyond the Catholic Church."Paris gears up for influxMassive crowds are expected for the pope's visit. Some 600,000 people who were able to get tickets will fill the entire Champs-Elysees, going right up to the Arc de Triomphe. Many more are expected to show up without tickets.Authorities have announced that a number of metro stations will be closed. Across the city, churches have been draped with large portraits of the pope and Vatican flags. Security forces are gearing up for a major challenge.With France's presidential election just over six months away, the visit comes at a delicate time. The left, Roy said, "appreciates Leo's personality but is skeptical about the state's involvement in organizing the reception."Those on the far right, he continued, welcomed the visibility of Catholicism but had objected, for example, to an interfaith meeting planned in the eastern city of Metz, which they say places Islam on an equal footing with Christianity.Because of the separation of church and state, the president will not be able to attend the large public Masses.Leo's visit is likely to boost the pope's profile in the country, which last saw a papal state visit in 2008 when Benedict XVI traveled to Paris and Lourdes, the world-famous pilgrimage site in the country's southwest. He drew smaller crowds than those expected for Pope Leo.His successor, Pope Francis, visited Strasbourg in 2014 and Ajaccio in Corsica in 2024 on one-day trips, and in 2023 he spent a night in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille. But each time, he came for a specific occasion rather than visiting the country as a whole. In his speeches to the European Parliament and Council of Europe in Strasbourg, Francis criticized the migration policies of what he described as an "aged and weary" Europe.Roy described the contrasting perspectives of recent popes. He said John Paul II, pope from 1978 to 2005, viewed Christianity as "primarily European," while Francis saw it as "more shaped by the Global South."This, Roy argued, explained Francis' "certain disregard for Europe." Leo was likely to assume the middle ground, while extending his predecessor's message, Roy said."He affirms the universality of the Catholic Church, while also recognizing Europe's weight within that universality."Europe's key role for the popeFor Augsburg-based church historian and papal expert Jörg Ernesti, Europe has remained "the most important political point of reference for popes since the late 19th century," despite the growing internationalism of Catholicism. Ernesti pointed to the demographic shift: In 1900, more than two-thirds of all Catholics lived in Europe, he said; today, the figure is only around 20%.This internationalization had also shaped the College of Cardinals, albeit with a time lag. "While Europeans have historically always made up the majority, they now account for just 39%," he said.During his four-day visit, Leo is scheduled to deliver 15 speeches and homilies. Most of those in Paris will be aimed at wider French society and its political leaders, while the large Masses and events in Lourdes will focus primarily on France's Catholics.The most keenly awaited speech is one scheduled for the final day in Metz, which French President Emmanuel Macron will introduce. It is titled "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity."The choice of Metz itself is symbolic. Once a center of the Carolingian Empire, the city has changed language and allegiance several times over the centuries, at times being German, at others French.While at the Robert Schuman Convention Center, Leo will be able to invoke the name of the man behind the building. Born in Luxembourg in 1886, Robert Schuman was a French statesman who had inherited his father's German citizenship at birth. In the aftermath of World War II, Schuman was an early advocate of Franco-German reconciliation. He pushed for a new, united Europe and in 1958 became the first president of the newly established European Parliament. After his death in 1963, he was buried in a small church in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz.For Pope Leo, Roy said, "Europe is a real entity that must be sustained and developed beyond nationalism." That, he said, "has always been the message of the Catholic Church since World War II. It is Schuman's message."Roy will be watching closely to see whether, and how openly, Pope Leo criticizes populism and nationalism in his call to strengthen the EU and whether he will speak about a form of nationalist Catholicism found in France. He said that defenders of the traditional Latin Mass were not infrequently "identitarian nationalists or even close to far-right circles."Leo to meet abuse survivorsIt's hard to imagine a papal trip without mention of the long-running issue of abuse. When Pope Benedict visited France in 2008, he did not take the chance to meet any survivors of sexual abuse in the French Catholic Church. His successors did, though the institution has been slow to confront its past amid a spate of new scandals.This time, a meeting with survivors is on the pope's agenda in Lourdes. But something else has changed. During the pontificates of Benedict and Francis, those who met with them were usually not named. At times, it appeared that access to the Vatican came in exchange for silence. In France, the seven survivors who will meet Leo have spoken out together ahead of the meeting, with five of them also making their names public."Dialogue does not mean approval," they said. "Being received does not mean giving up our demands." The issue is likely to remain a thorny challenge for the Catholic Church — in France and elsewhere for a long time to come.Read: UNGA: Mahmoud Abbas Calls for Palestinian Self-DeterminationClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: Pope Leo XIV is expected to draw huge crowds during his visit to France. As part of his trip, he's also set to address Europe's future and more.

news.title: Melania Trump gives rare insight into relationship with son Barron amid reports he's 'reclusive'
news.text:
First Lady Melania Trump has offered a rare, candid look into her dynamic with her 20-year-old son, Barron, acknowledging that the intense demands of the White House have significantly reduced their time together as a family.

Appearing on Fox Business’s The Big Money Show on Wednesday evening, the 56-year-old was asked by co-host Taylor Riggs how she balances state dinners, charity initiatives, and executive events while trying to maintain traditional routines, such as Sunday night family dinners.

Melania conceded that the reality of presidential life makes regular family gatherings nearly impossible, emphasizing that planning ahead is essential when everyone's schedule is pulled in different directions.

"It’s good to schedule, it’s always good because everybody’s so busy," she explained. "My husband is working — sometimes he’s in the Oval Office until 9:30 at night, so do you wait [until then to] have dinner? You don’t. He’s busy, I’m busy too."

The First Lady did not shy away from the personal toll of those long working hours, directly noting the strain on their private home life.

"It’s less and less family time, [and there's] suffering because of it. But that’s okay. We are here to work, to do a good job, and that’s what matters," she said.

Turning to Barron, who is currently studying at New York University, Melania acknowledged that her only child is developing his own independence into adulthood. "Barron is already a young man, so sometimes he’s maybe even happy that I just want to do my stuff. And that’s okay," she added with a smile.

The First Lady’s remarks come amid recent reports describing the 20-year-old as increasingly protective of his privacy. 

Insiders have characterized him as living inside a rigid security bubble, particularly in the wake of escalating political violence and heightened threats directed toward his father.

Donald Trump has survived multiple assassination attempts, while Barron himself has become the subject of overseas targeting, including a hostile propaganda clip released by Iranian regime hardliners that claimed to track his whereabouts. 

The college student was also deeply affected by the September 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, an acquaintance he had previously asked his father to introduce him to over lunch.

Addressing ongoing scrutiny of the student's lifestyle, the First Lady’s office previously issued a firm boundary: "In light of recent threats, the East Wing asks that any details concerning his private life be excluded from all coverage."

Barron has kept public outings strictly limited to heavily secured occasions, such as the UFC Freedom 250 bouts on the South Lawn in June and the FIFA World Cup 2026 final in New Jersey in July.
news.summary: First Lady Melania Trump admitted her family time is 'suffering' amid packed schedules, sharing rare comments about son Barron.

news.title: US tech titans attend Trump-Xi dinner. Who wasn’t invited?
news.text:
Virtually all of America’s most powerful technology executives joined US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a lavish White House state dinner on Thursday, as artificial intelligence emerged as a major theme of the Chinese leader’s visit.

The black-tie dinner in the White House East Room brought together more than 130 guests, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.

Apple chairman Tim Cook, AMD chief Lisa Su, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan and Dell Technologies chief Michael Dell were also among those invited. Major finance and industrial executives, including JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg, attended as well.

One notable Silicon Valley name was missing, however. Anthropic – the developer of the Claude AI models and one of OpenAI’s biggest US rivals – had no representative. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, has been among the industry’s more vocal advocates of tighter safeguards around increasingly powerful AI systems.

Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel was also absent, though he was in Berlin that evening receiving the 2026 Axel Springer Award. His CIA-seeded data-mining giant has grown into one of Silicon Valley’s biggest defense-tech players, supplying AI and analytics software to all six branches of the US military, as well as the FBI, NSA and DIA. Its technology is also used by NATO and the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, while the company has faced sustained criticism over its expanding role in surveillance and AI-enabled warfare.

Intel, IBM and Oracle were also absent from the guest list, which otherwise featured many of America’s biggest technology and AI companies.

There was also a conspicuous absence on the other side of the table: no Chinese corporate executives were listed, despite earlier expectations that business leaders could accompany Xi. Instead, his delegation at the dinner was composed of senior Chinese officials.

The concentration of American tech executives came as Trump and Xi discussed the increasingly intense US-China competition in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.

Earlier on Thursday, Xi said both countries had a responsibility to ensure AI remained “under human control” and was developed for the benefit of people.

Trump, meanwhile, said AI – which he has increasingly referred to as “superintelligence” – was high on the summit agenda, while reiterating his opposition to slowing development through extensive regulation. Washington has also proposed establishing a mechanism allowing the two countries to notify each other about serious AI-related incidents, an idea discussed by senior economic officials ahead of the summit.

The dinner followed roughly 90 minutes of talks between Trump and Xi at the White House, where the two sides also addressed trade, Taiwan and the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Washington and Beijing agreed earlier this week to extend their existing trade truce by two months while negotiations continue.

Trump used his toast to emphasize cooperation despite the rivalry, saying the two leaders represent “different systems” but could continue building a relationship promoting prosperity and security.

In his toast, Xi said China’s pursuit of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda “can surely be mutually reinforcing.”

The dinner capped a day of elaborate ceremonies at the White House, including a military review and a separate flyover featuring a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors. Trump also revealed that earlier in the day, he had presented Xi with a roughly three-foot-tall bald eagle statue designed by an American artist in collaboration with the president and first lady, calling the bird a symbol of America’s “free and soaring spirit.” Details of Xi’s gift were not immediately disclosed.

The White House guest list featured leaders of America’s top AI firms as Washington and Beijing grapple with an intensifying tech rivalry

news.title: Ivanka Trump takes front-row seat to welcome Xi in dress by Chinese designer Guo Pei
news.text:
The US president’s eldest daughter Ivanka Trump had a front-row seat at a White House welcome ceremony for President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan on Thursday, wearing a dress by Chinese fashion designer Guo Pei.
Trump, in a robin’s egg blue dress and matching jacket, and her 15-year-old daughter Arabella Kushner occupied a prominent position at the ceremony, alongside Vice-President J.D. Vance and his wife, Usha Vance.
The arrangement drew attention since members of Donald Trump’s cabinet – including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth – were seated further back.
US media reported that Ivanka Trump’s striking blue gown and jacket with silver embroidery were designed by Guo, while her daughter wore a white belted midi dress by London-based fashion brand Self-Portrait.

The choice of a Beijing-based designer as well as the seating arrangement reflected the Trump family’s personal and commercial ties with China. During Donald Trump’s first term as president, his daughter Ivanka was an unpaid adviser and became an important conduit for Chinese officials in Washington.
When Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan visited the United States in April 2017, Ivanka’s daughter Arabella performed the traditional Chinese ballad “Mo Li Hua” (Jasmine Flower) and recited Tang dynasty poetry in Chinese.
Later that year in Beijing, President Trump showed Xi private video recordings of his granddaughter addressing the Chinese leader and his wife as “Grandpa Xi” and “Grandma Peng”.

Meanwhile, Ivanka Trump secured multiple trademark approvals in China during her father’s presidency in 2018, sparking widespread discussion about potential conflicts of interest. Trademarks covered standard fashion and lifestyle goods and also services like voting machines and nursing homes.
She shut down her business in mid-2018, saying that she would focus on her government work. In 2022, Ivanka Trump announced she was stepping away from politics and leaving the political arena.
There was symbolism in wearing a dress for Thursday’s ceremony by Chinese designer Guo. news.title: Beyond high-profile wars, a worldwide battle for critical minerals
news.text:
According to Pakistani
media, the militants who stormed a lithium mining site in
Balochistan last month had a simple message as they destroyed
equipment and briefly detained employees: they were no longer
prepared to tolerate mining operations in the region, and
foreign and local mining firms ​should stay away.

As wars in the Middle East and Ukraine grabbed headlines and
the United States and China navigated their still largely
bloodless face-off, culminating in the meeting of President
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping this ‌week, a host of other
overlapping confrontations over resources have ranged elsewhere
in the world throughout 2026.

Behind the scenes, the US, European Union and Pacific
governments, ​particularly Japan, South Korea, Australia and
Taiwan, are already locked in a still-escalating high-stakes
race to uncouple themselves from China when it comes to the key
resources ⁠driving modern tech.

Rare earths and minerals continue to fuel conflict in
central Africa, while Sudan’s ongoing civil war is now largely
fuelled by gold smuggling that fills the coffers of groups
intent on ethnic violence.

Some of that will have been discussed in New York this week
at the annual United Nations General Assembly bringing world
leaders together – but much of this global confrontation now
takes place behind the scenes, albeit with starkly rising

In ‌the Gulf, the US-Iran conflict sparked by the launch of
the US-Israeli "Operation Epic Fury" – now widened to include a
worsening face-off between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi
rebels – now threatens an energy supply shock that might
significantly derail global growth.

In the short term, significant amounts of the energy of the
UN gathering were consumed by ‌discussions over the safety of
fast-evolving artificial intelligence models, with OpenAI Chief
Executive Sam Altman and others briefing the Security Council.
Discussions over Ukraine have also included a potential
suspension by both ‌sides ⁠of attacks on energy infrastructure.

In the background, however, the at least equally high-stakes
confrontation taking place is over the raw materials necessary
for that ongoing computing ⁠and wider technological revolution –
including copper for almost every form of circuitry, lithium
batteries and a host of other rarer earths and other minerals.

In June, the European Commission joined the US State
Department-coordinated “Pax Silica”, a Washington-led collective
of more than two dozen nations that commenced with an agreement
between the US and Japan in September and has expanded since to
include much of Europe, as well as key Pacific allies.

Still, according to consultancy AlixPartners, Beijing still
accounts for up to ​70% of rare earth mining, 85% of refining
capability and 90% of rare ‌earth metal alloy and magnet
production. According to industry experts, the latter remains a
pinch point for both aerospace and cutting-edge chip
manufacturers – and so far, foreign diplomats in Washington say
the US continues to struggle to regain that initiative.

That makes the battle for resources in places like Pakistan
and central Asia particularly important – even while the limits
of reporting and established fact can make that hard to track.
What is clear, however, is that they are already very much part
of that wider confrontation.

BALOCHISTAN MINING TARGETED

According to global monitoring NGO ACLED – ‌which stands for
Armed Conflict Location and Event Data – mining interests in
Balochistan have been targeted on at least 40 separate occasions
so far in 2026.

Local media now detail ​a wider range of incidents taking
place almost every day, including an ambush and firefight of
almost three dozen mining vehicles at the end of August that
left at least 13 militants dead.

Other stories tell of suspected militants detained and then
found dead, victims of suspected extrajudicial killings by
government personnel or private ⁠security.

Who is behind the several overlapping groups of ethnic
Baloch militants remains hotly disputed. Pakistan routinely
blames India’s Research and Analysis Wing intelligence agency,
known as RAW, for coordinating and arming the attacks, something
India denies. The region is the poorest in Pakistan, with
guerrilla fighters reportedly crossing the border from Iran and
Afghanistan.

What is not in doubt is their mounting opposition to Chinese
mining interests, which has intensified ‌sharply in recent years.
The US has condemned the attacks as terrorism, but not commented
in more detail – although the government in Islamabad has
increasingly presented itself to the Trump administration as an
appealing partner, including as a source of resources.

Visiting Trump in the Oval Office in October 2025,
Pakistan's military chief and de facto ruler Asim Munir brought
with him a wooden display case of minerals before signing a $500
million memorandum of understanding. While mining currently
makes up less than 1% of Pakistani GDP, the government claims it
has as much as $6 trillion in undeveloped reserves.

Amongst the largest projects is the Reko Dik gold and copper
mine, unusually for Pakistan one by Canadian firm Barrick rather
than a China-based conglomerate. The multi-vehicle convoy
ambushed at the end of August was returning from the mine, due
to enter production in 2029.

OTHER RESOURCE FLASHPOINTS

Other nations increasingly in the crosshairs of global
resource competition include those in Central Asia. In June,
Kazakhstan became the first nation in that ‌region to sign up to
the US-run “Pax Silica” – but it appeared to alienate Washington
by also joining the China-run World Artificial Intelligence
Cooperation Organisation (WAICO) barely three weeks later.

That prompted an immediate warning from the US State
Department that membership ​of the “Pax Silica” collective was
irreconcilable with joining rival Chinese entities. But in
reality, Washington will always seek to continue to build new
resource deals with the Kazakhstan government, which oversees
some of the world’s largest stockpiles of uranium as well as
chromite, copper, beryllium, tantalum, lead and zinc.

The US hosted all five major ⁠Central Asian powers at a
critical mineral summit last November, striking further deals
with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. South Korea hosted its own
critical mineral summit this month with several Central Asian
governments, while Japanese media ⁠reported this week that Tokyo
would launch its own strategy next year with a similar goal.

Japan is also now at the forefront of what is now often
described as “urban mining”.

In April, a quartet of Japanese companies announced they
would use robots to recover neodymium magnets critical to
computer hard drives from old air-conditioners. Other firms are
pushing ahead ‌with undersea remote mining projects to tap
resources previously unreachable.

The Trump administration also has a range of commercial and
diplomatic outreach underway in Latin America, keen to push back
against the previous dominance of Chinese extractive firms in
the “Lithium Triangle” of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia –
although despite that, Chinese trade with South American nations
has continued to rise sharply in the current ​year.

In the Oval Office this week, Trump and Xi might have tried
to look like two geopolitical titans dividing the world between
them. But the reality on the ground is already considerably
messier, and the scramble for resources in the new industrial
age is only just beginning.

(The opinions expressed here are those Peter Apps, the author, a
columnist for Reuters.)

Published on September 25, 2026
news.summary: Critical minerals are emerging as a new source of geopolitical tension, with governments seeking secure supplies for technology and industry

news.title: Michael Goodwin: Netanyahu entered a hostile environment — and met the moment with a speech that can only be called a success
news.text:
It is a given that many media and political descriptions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech to the United Nations will call it fiery and defiant.

And so it was — and so it had to be. 

Both the content and the sometimes-harsh tone were essential if he was to capture the moment and the point of his appearance.

Once again and always, Israel is in a fight for its existence, and finds itself being abandoned by former allies in Europe and increasingly isolated on the world stage.

Given those circumstances, nobody of sane and fair mind could seriously expect the Jewish state’s leader to come to a hostile United Nations bearing a bouquet of olive branches.

Not to mention the fact that New York is now led by a mayor who is hostile to him personally and to Israel’s existence as the Jewish homeland.

Had he delivered a subservient and apologetic tone on either front, Netanyahu would have been deserving of a serious head-shrinking examination.

Skills on full display

And he would have faced hostile crowds when he returned home to Tel Aviv, as well as almost certain defeat in next month’s elections.

And so the timing of the address dictated that it inevitably would be a plea to Israeli voters as well as a forceful message of defiance to the nations of the world — and Mayor Mamdani.

My view is that Netanyahu achieved a smashing success on all fronts. 

Not that he necessarily changed a single mind anywhere, but that he made the best possible case for himself and his tiny and beleaguered country.

As for the huge number of delegates who noisily walked out as Netanyahu took the podium, he called them “moral cowards.” 

True that, but they are also fools, for they missed a master class in how to simultaneously fight for your political future and your country.

There are good reasons why Netanyahu has been prime minister for more years than any of Israel’s previous leaders. 

He’s a skilled tactician and has earned the gravitas that his long list of failed opponents have never been able to match.

He’s also a brilliant speaker — no teleprompter needed Thursday — and has a clear-eyed view of his nation’s place in the world and its strengths and weaknesses.

His theme, the very heart of the address, was that Israel must win every war it faces “because we have no other choice.”

Defeat would mean total destruction and even elimination, the goal of Israel’s enemies now and throughout human history.

He came to that survival of the fittest theme with a tender story about his late brother, Yonatan. 

The prime minister said his brother used those exact words during the Six-Day War in 1967 and echoed them when they met not long before Yonatan was killed in 1976 while heroically leading the rescue of more than 100 Israeli hostages whose plane had been hijacked by terrorists and sat on the ground in the airport in Entebbe, Uganda.

From there, he cited Israel’s military prowess going back to earlier wars for its modern creation and against Arab neighbors, and its current role in fighting alongside the United States against a despotic Iran.

From his unique vantage point, it is a long “battle against barbarians.”

He also directly took on the false claims that Israel was guilty of committing “genocide” in Gaza and declared that the Israel Defense Forces are “the most moral army in the world.”

Its opponents, he said, hate Israel and hate America.

Saluted Trump

That is not to say that all criticism of him and the Jewish nation qualify as antisemitic, but there is no better example of his point than Iran’s long game of conquest.

Ever since the Islamic revolution nearly 50 years ago, the mad mullahs and their thuggish agents and brutal armies have called Israel the “Little Satan” and America the “Great Satan” — and vowed to eliminate both.

They have oppressed and slaughtered their own people, with tens of thousands executed and even tortured for daring to protest the government’s inept handling of the economy and even delivering the basics, such as electricity and clean drinking water.

Donald Trump is the first American president to treat the Iranian brutality at home and threats abroad with the seriousness they deserve, especially since Iran embarked on its quest for nuclear weapons decades ago.

Netanyahu saluted Trump for their partnership in the effort, even though Trump has lately been putting some distance between them as the president fights for his own standing and his Republican Party in the November midterms.

The irony is that both men face political peril in part because of their alliance against Iran and its brutal proxies, and that peril explains Netanyahu’s defiant speech.

More fully, he is battling for his political life in large part because many Israeli voters hold him responsible for failing to see the growing Hamas threat that led to the terrorists’ brutal invasion on Oct. 7, 2023.

With 1,200 people killed, including many women and even children, it was the bloodiest day for Jews since the Holocaust.

Netanyahu’s ability to put off a national inquiry about what went wrong and why the invasion was a complete surprise to the military has angered many voters across the political spectrum and could cost him his job next month.

In a clear instance of how he tried to rally his political base while at the UN, he criticized as overblown and exaggerated the widespread international criticism about Israeli settlers attacking and harassing Palestinians in the West Bank.

‘Can’t silence truth’

He put some distance between himself and the violent settlers, saying “I can’t stand them” as he touched his chest.

That was mild compared to his contempt for Mayor Mamdani, saying that since his election, “many Jews don’t feel in New York.”

It was a fitting broadside, given Mamdani’s bigoted attempt to have Netanyahu arrested as a “war criminal,” and the recent rise of antisemitism in what had been for decades the safest city in the world for Jews.

“Shame on you,” he said, and even threw a barbed jab at Mamdani’s wife for social media posts where she seemingly approved of Muslim violence against Jews.

“You tried to stop me,” he said, “but you can’t silence the truth.”

Hallelujah to that.
news.summary: It is a given that many media and political descriptions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech to the United Nations will call it fiery and defiant.
news.author: Michael Goodwin

New Democrat Leader David Eby said his party is the clear choice for standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump, while the British Columbia Conservatives would turn the province into "America Junior," complete with health-care privatization.

The day after calling a snap election set for Oct. 24, citing Trump's threats, Eby touted his government's success in recruiting American health-care workers and said the NDP would triple the funding for the campaign to $15 million.

"When we put forward a $5 million campaign, just $5 million, to recruit these health-care workers, the Conservatives called it irresponsible," Eby told a campaign stop in front of the the Peace Arch border crossing in Surrey, B.C., on Wednesday.

The campaign resulted in the hiring of 800 health-care workers from south of the border and ultimately saved the province money, Eby said.

"It costs us hundreds of thousands of dollars to train a new doctor or a new nurse."

Eby said the NDP has set a goal of recruiting 2,400 more health workers from across the border in a renewed campaign that would expand into Republican-controlled states, with laws that restrict the provision of reproductive health care.

"If we turn our province into America Junior, we put all of that at risk," he said.

Eby questioned why a health-care worker would uproot their life and move to B.C. if the province had the same hallmarks as the American system, characterizing it as "private health-care with big corporations" and "culture wars" dictating treatment.

The Conservatives under former leader John Rustad had campaigned on a promise to expand private clinics to help fix what he called a system in crisis.

Eby also highlighted the prosperity agreement between B.C. and Ottawa, unveiled in July, saying it comes with federal funding to advance major projects including liquefied natural gas facilities and the expansions of a mine and several ports.

Eby said the same Conservatives running under Lorne Doerkson, the interim leader, had opposed the deal with Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal government.

"Whether it's any one of the last four leaders of the Conservatives in the last 10 months, the ideas are the same," he said.

A Conservative news release from the time, quoting two of the legislators who flanked Doerkson as he addressed reporters in Vancouver on Tuesday, criticized the agreement for maintaining the tanker ban along B.C.'s North Coast.

news.title: Iran Offers 7-Day Plan to Restart US Talks, Reopen Strait of Hormuz
news.text:
Iran has offered a seven-day plan to the United States aimed at creating a pathway back to negotiations, with the proposal involving the reopening of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the proposal in New York amid diplomatic efforts on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. According to reports, Tehran has conveyed the plan to Washington through intermediaries.

Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz at the end of the seven-day period if certain conditions are met, after which negotiations would resume with the aim of reaching a broader agreement. US-Iran Talks at UNGA: Steve Witkoff Calls Mediated Discussions ‘Constructive and Promising’.

Iran's Seven-Day Plan For US Talks

Araghchi said the proposal was similar in several respects to the memorandum of understanding reached between the US and Iran in June. Iran has been seeking an end to US military pressure and the blockade affecting Iranian ports as part of efforts to restart diplomacy. Earlier reports said Tehran had offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted the blockade.

The latest proposal adds a clearer diplomatic sequence: conditions would be met, the waterway would be reopened, and talks would then restart on outstanding issues, including Iran's nuclear programme.

Strait of Hormuz At Centre Of Negotiations

The Strait of Hormuz, a major global energy route, has become a central issue in the negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Reuters reported on September 24 that US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased arrangement under which Iran would reopen the waterway while the United States would lift its economic blockade of Iran. The discussions were taking place in New York through diplomatic channels. Iran has previously linked the reopening of the strait to the easing of US military and economic pressure. Tehran has also demanded an end to what it describes as US intervention and attacks against Iran. Iran Sets 7 Conditions for US Talks: What Are Tehran’s Demands To End War?.

Nuclear Talks Could Restart

A key element of the seven-day proposal is the possibility of restarting negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme. Araghchi said the proposal would create a pathway for comprehensive discussions after the Strait of Hormuz is reopened. The initiative comes after months of conflict and diplomatic deadlock between Washington and Tehran. Iran has maintained that a return to diplomacy requires concrete steps from the US, while Washington has continued to seek assurances over Iran's actions and the broader regional security situation.

UN General Assembly Provides Diplomatic Opening

The proposal comes as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials are in New York for the UN General Assembly. US and Iranian officials have held indirect discussions through mediators during the gathering. Qatar, Pakistan and Egypt have been involved in diplomatic efforts aimed at narrowing differences between the two sides. Earlier reports said Pezeshkian was not expected to hold a direct meeting with US President Donald Trump, although Iranian officials indicated that negotiations could advance if Washington demonstrated sufficient commitment.

US-Iran Talks Remain Uncertain

The seven-day proposal represents a new diplomatic initiative, but major differences remain unresolved. The Strait of Hormuz, the US blockade, military operations, economic pressure and Iran's nuclear programme are all part of the broader dispute. Reuters reported that both sides remain cautious about giving up negotiating leverage while exploring a possible phased arrangement. For now, the proposal provides a framework for renewed negotiations rather than a concluded agreement. Further discussions through mediators are expected to determine whether Washington and Tehran can agree on the conditions needed to implement the seven-day plan.

news.title: ‘Washington, Tehran exploring phased way out of war’
news.text:
