news.summary: The Israeli prime minister addressed world leaders amid international criticism of Israel’s military actions and growing focus on the Gaza war

news.title: Trump offers Xi state dinner guests first-ever tour of ballroom construction site: ‘Special treat’
news.text:
Donald Trump couldn’t help but offer guests at his state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping a first-ever tour of his ballroom construction site. 

The president loves to boast to the White House press corps and his Truth Social followers about his passion projects around Washington, D.C., especially the massive White House ballroom being built. Now, in front of an international audience, Trump has offered to share a glimpse of what he called a “clean and sparkly” construction site. 

“And if I could go off script just for a second,” Trump said as dinner guests in the East Room of the White House laughed. “But as a special treat in honor of President Xi and Madame [Liyuan] Peng. I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back.”

“It's one year away from completion — the new ballroom that you've heard about, and you will see something that I think you will really love.”

The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom will fit 650 seats, compared to the 200 seats in the East Room. Trump has said construction will cost about $400 million and that he and other donors would pay for it.

But the project’s contractor told the administration that it would cost $600 million, with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.

The Trump administration has also been challenged in court over whether it had the authority to tear down the East Wing last October to build the ballroom without Congressional approval. The Supreme Court ruled last month that the president can continue with construction for the time being.

“You'll be the first people to step foot on that, and we'll do that maybe after we're finished with the entertainment tonight. Anybody [who] wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkly, it's our honor to have you do so,” Trump told his dinner guests. 

The official delegations from the US and China attended the state dinner. Some notable names on the guest list included first lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Trump was photographed next to Melania while waiting to greet Xi and his wife Peng at the White House ahead of the dinner. Makeup was caked on his left hand, which he often uses to cover up bruising. 

The Trump administration has said the black and blue on the back of his hands is due to frequent handshaking and aspirin use.

Several of America’s tech leaders, such as SpaceX’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, were also in attendance Thursday night amid an AI race with China. 

During the legal fight to build his ballroom, Trump argued that it was needed for national security. Underneath the East Wing sits a bunker dating back to 1942, after the U.S. entered World War II. In court filings, the Trump administration noted that bomb shelters, military installations and a medical facility would be added to the bunker during construction. 

So when Trump suggested officials from China, an adversary of the U.S., tour the construction site, it raised some eyebrows. 

“Of the security bunker? Seems suboptimal,” Reuters journalist Charlie Szymanski wrote on Bluesky.

“Guided tour of the super secure and classified military ballroom for officials of a foreign unfriendly nation. Totally reasonable,” another Bluesky user, Jeff Domingues, posted. 

One X user wrote, “Let’s take the leader of China into the ballroom that doubles as a military bunker! Great idea Don!”

Melania led the preparations for the state dinner, which included a menu that the White House said had a “subtle Chinese influence.” For the main course, guests enjoyed sesame-crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy. 

Entertainment for the night was headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s second inauguration. Guests were also treated to performances by military ensembles.

“Thank you, Mr. President and Mrs. Trump, for extending to my wife and me your gracious hospitality and thoughtful arrangements,” Xi said at the dinner through an interpreter. “You make us feel truly at home.”

“I would also like to extend my sincere greetings to Americans from all sectors of society who care about China-U.S. relations and support the further growth of our bilateral ties.”
news.summary: The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom being built in the White House’s East Wing is expected to cost hundreds of millions of dollars
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Xi to invite 100,000 young Americans to China for study, exchanges over five years
news.text:
China’s President Xi Jinping on Thursday said one lakh young Americans will be invited to visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years.

The announcement by Xi at the White House here came against the backdrop of a similar announcement made in 2023, under which 50,000 young Americans were invited for exchanges and study over a five-year period. The target was achieved this year ahead of schedule.

“The hope of China-US relationship lies in our people, and its future lies with the young. I am glad to announce an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study in the coming five years,” Xi said.

Xi invokes shared World War II history

The Chinese leader made a reference to the Second World War when Chinese and Americans fought “shoulder-to-shoulder” against the “fascist” aggression.

“Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people,” Xi said.

“Ladies and gentlemen, dear friends, achieving the Great Rejuvenation of the Chinese Nation and making America great again can go hand in hand. Let us meet the people’s expectations and show our historical initiative. Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples, and work together to build a better world,” Xi said.

Trump highlights US-China wartime ties

Earlier, US President Donald Trump had referred to the US role in helping China in the Second World War against Japanese aggression.

Trump listed issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence and said the decisions he and Xi make in these areas can promote peace and prosperity for decades to come.

“We focus on our common interests, and I’m confident there is much we can achieve throughout history,” he said.

Trump recalls Flying Tigers

“Pursuit of those common interests has connected our people across the vast oceans of big, tremendous distances and many differences, and even made us allies in World War II,” Trump said.

“Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II. Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country, that legendary Flying Tigers group. They were just unbelievable,” Trump said.

Trump cites ‘Gung Ho’ phrase

“And it was the United States Marines’ encounter with Chinese people that inspired the Marines to adopt a Chinese phrase they still use today, ‘Gung Ho.’ The Marines use it as an expression of great enthusiasm, but in Chinese it literally means working together,” Trump said.

news.summary: The announcement came after an earlier five-year initiative inviting 50,000 young Americans achieved its target ahead of schedule

news.title: Xi Pushes Trump To Oppose' Taiwan Independence In Rare Call
news.text: Chinese leader Xi Jinping pressed the US to outright "oppose" Taiwan independence, marking his first public call for Donald Trump to change Washington's decades-old stance on the self-ruled island.During their inaugural White House summit on Thursday, Xi urged the US leader to "adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence," according to the official Xinhua News Agency. That wording is stronger than the Biden administration's previous statement that US officials "do not support" the island seeking formal independence.Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has made bringing Taiwan under China's control a key goal and vowed to achieve it someday, by force if necessary. As the Chinese leader heads toward an expected fourth term in office, he's ramping up diplomatic pressure to isolate the democratic chip hub and block future weapons sales from Washington.The US still hasn't released a readout from the meeting, which lasted less than two hours, meaning it isn't clear how Trump responded to Xi's request. China privately asked the Trump administration to declare it "opposes" Taiwan independence back in 2025, a person familiar with the matter said at the time.The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.ALSO READ: Trump Says US, China Want To Leave AI Exactly Where It Is' Amid Global Safety Debate"While this may appear a semantic shift, the impact would be meaningful," said Bloomberg Economics' Jennifer Welch, who served as director for China and Taiwan on the National Security Council under the previous Biden and Trump administrations. China would use any switch in language from Trump to undermine Taiwan's confidence in US support, she added."Opposing Taiwan independence implies an active effort to contain what Beijing sees as pro-independence forces," Welch said.Trump has already delayed a planned $14 billion arms package for Taiwan for months. After his last meeting with Xi in Beijing, Trump described that deal as "a very good negotiating chip" for the US - remarks that rattled Taipei. Any change in wording would fan concerns that Washington's position on the democracy of 23 million people is becoming a bargaining chip in US-China ties.Taiwan SpotlightXi has rarely made such an explicit call to an American leader. The last time came in November 2024, when he told outgoing President Joe Biden if the US wanted peace it should "oppose Taiwan independence," during their final face-to-face.Chinese state media released Xi's remarks on Taiwan hours before its full readout on Thursday, throwing a spotlight on Beijing's top red line issue. That followed a similar pattern to the last Trump-Xi summit in May, when China warned mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to "clashes " between the superpowers in a statement issued while talks were ongoing.Xi entered his first state visit to America in 11 years emboldened after last year exposing US reliance on China's rare earths, a move that enabled Beijing to push back against Trump's triple-digit tariffs. Those minerals are critical for making everything from missiles to mobile phones and have been key in keeping a lid on further US export controls.Trump has given Xi an unprecedented welcome, becoming the first US president to greet a Chinese counterpart on the tarmac. Tonight, the Republic leader will host only his second state dinner of this term for Xi - one of America's biggest economic and military rivals.In a boon to Beijing, Trump's comments on Taiwan have marked a departure from Biden, who claimed he'd defend the island from any invasion by China. The Republican leader has urged officials in Taipei to step up their ability to defend themselves.ALSO READ: 'Always Under Human Control': Xi Jinping Says US, China Must Jointly Steer AI For GoodHandling the Taiwan question with prudence will "lay a solid foundation for strategic cooperation between China and the US," Xi said on Thursday.Ryan Hass, director of the China Center at the Brookings Institution in Washington, said Xi was trying to link the concept of "constructive strategic stability" to opposing Taiwan independence. That slogan was unveiled by Chinese officials at the leaders' summit in May to define a new era in ties."The key acid test will be what Trump says on Taiwan," Hass added. "Not just what Xi urges Trump to endorse."(This story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Trump-Xi state dinner: Tech billionaires, lavish menu and White House pageantry in focus
news.text:
A tech-heavy guest list, the fashion choices of those on it, who sits where, their body language throughout the night and what’s on the menu: these are the softer — often and glitzier — details of diplomacy.

Thursday’s state dinner for China’s leader Xi Jinping featured a cavalcade of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that excite President Donald Trump, who has a reputation for revelling in hosting parties.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman signed autographs as he arrived at the White House. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang chose a tuxedo over his trademark black leather jacket. Bernard Arnault, the CEO of French luxury goods company LVMH, walked through black security fencing to get to the White House.

“Everyone wants to be there,” Trump said during this week’s UN General Assembly session. “It’s the hottest ticket in town.”

Xi and Trump face tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours — even as an ongoing, First Amendment fight over press access at the White House has unfolded. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal honouring Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, in the White House East Room.

Asked on Monday night who’d be in attendance, the president responded, “sort of everybody,” adding, “I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world and a lot more.”

Dinner signals warmth and connection

The dinner was expected to showcase “the positive vibes surrounding the visit” and indicate that “the president is very focused on signalling warmth and a close personal connection with Xi,” said Edgard Kagan, senior adviser and chair in China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

A lavish menu for Xi and guests

First lady Melania Trump’s menu features a first course of yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, fresh herbs, crispy pancetta and drizzled scallion oil.

After that, guests will get sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte. Dessert is vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House.

Trump seeks to match Beijing’s pageantry

The dinner comes after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their state visit guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.

During Thursday’s arrival ceremony, Trump and Xi reviewed troops with trumpets blaring and the US president saying, “From the time of my first election in 2016 President Xi and I have forged a friendship.”

Technology titans join the guest list

Thursday’s dinner will include an abundance of technology industry titans, including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai of Google, OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Michael Dell, the CEO of Dell Technologies.

During his own visit to Beijing in May, Xi treated Trump to a state dinner that unfolded beneath grand chandeliers at the Great Hall of the People. That event included many tech luminaries who are likely to be at the White House this time, such as Tim Cook, formerly Apple’s CEO and Musk.

Trump has since begun referring to the White House ballroom that he’s building as the “Great Hall of the United States” to rival where he dined in China.

“This is a very large hall,” Trump recently said of the Great Hall of the People before adding, “But we’re gonna top it.”

Trump once criticised state dinner pomp

In 2015, as then-President Barack Obama was preparing to host Xi for a state visit, Trump — in the midst of his first run for president — criticised all the hubbub.

“Just take them to McDonald’s and go back to the negotiating table,” Trump said then, during a rally in South Carolina. He later conceded on Fox News Channel that Xi might at least be worthy of getting “probably a double-size Big Mac.”

Xi’s 2017 visit to Mar-a-Lago

Xi visited Trump in 2017 for the first time. But the White House said the Chinese wanted that meeting to happen at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, viewed as a more relaxed setting that might defuse some of the high expectations of a formal summit in Washington.

A dinner interrupted by Syria strikes

A dearth of pageantry didn’t mean a lack of extraordinary moments, however, underscoring just how important having China’s leader dine with Trump can be.

Later recounting the incident to Fox News Channel, Trump said he sprung a surprise on Xi just after dinner, noting that the US was striking Syria as the pair was having “the most beautiful piece of chocolate cake that you’ve ever seen, and President Xi was enjoying it.”

Trump said he told Xi that US forces had “just fired 59 missiles” and that China’s president “was eating his cake. And he was silent.”

Published on September 25, 2026
news.summary: Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX, Google and OpenAI executives were among prominent technology figures expected at the high-profile White House gathering

news.title: Al Michaels commits 'cardinal sin' on Thursday Night Football broadcast leaving viewers shocked
news.text:
Veteran broadcaster Al Michaels has come under fire from football fans after committing what viewers branded a 'cardinal sin' during Thursday Night Football. 

Calling the Atlanta Falcons' clash against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on Amazon Prime Video, the 81-year-old endured a nightmare start to the action. 

During the opening drive, Michaels attempted to recap the college journey of Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr – only to get his facts completely wrong.

In an attempt to set the scene, Michaels told viewers that Penix Jr had started his career at Indiana before having 'two great years at Oregon.' 

College football fans quickly seized on the glaring error, pointing out that Penix starred for the Washington Huskies – who are fierce rivals of the Oregon Ducks.

While Michaels later corrected himself and tried to move past the slip-up, the damage across social media was already done. 

Taking to X, one disgruntled fan wrote: 'Al Michaels just committed the cardinal sin of football, saying Michael Penix had 'two greats years at Oregon.' He corrected himself after my blood pressure had already spike.'

'Al Michaels is already drunk. He said Michael Penix went to Oregon when he actually went to Washington,' another user added on the social media platform.

Another wrote: 'Al Michaels just said Penix played at Oregon after Indiana. Flying out of the gate.'

'Al Michaels really just said 'started his career at Indiana, then two great years at Oregon' bruh Someone got in his ear to correct him right away, but confusing Washington for their rival won't make fans happy,' said one user. 

The embarrassing moment came just one week after Michaels took a brutal on-air shot at Donald Trump over failed $1 billion attempt to buy the Buffalo Bills. 

During last week's Thursday Night Football clash, Michaels said: 'There were basically three bidders. Pegula, who won it at [$1.4 billion]; a Toronto group, [rock star Jon] Bon Jovi was in it…

'And the other bidder, Donald J. Trump, who said publicly, "I'm gonna write a cashier's check for a billion dollars." The league said, "nah, we're good. We'll take Pegula."'

Pegula's 2014 purchase of the team represented Trump's fourth failed run at buying an NFL franchise, not including his doomed foray into the USFL.

Trump supporters quickly took offense at Michaels' comment.

'People watch football to escape all the bulls*** that goes on in the world,' one angry critic wrote on X. 'Nobody wants to hear that political nonsense.'

'lol am I supposed to care more about a guy that speaks on sports for a living or the sitting president?' another asked. 'F*** Al.'

One critic suggested Michaels 'retire because he's becoming more senile every week.'

'Remember,' they added, 'go woke go broke.
news.summary: Calling the Atlanta Falcons' clash against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on Amazon Prime Video, the 81-year-old endured a nightmare start to the action.

news.title: Trade, Taiwan And AI: Five Takeaways From Donald Trump, Xi Jinping Summit
news.text: US President Donald Trump hosted his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, for a lavish state dinner at the White House, followed by a day of pomp and ceremony that masked deep tensions between the rival nuclear superpowers. The tech-heavy event was attended by a cavalcade of billionaires, Washington power brokers, and business leaders, including Tesla's Elon Musk, Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, underscoring that trade and artificial intelligence were high on the agenda for Xi's visit."President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."The US leader has done his best to impress Xi, praising their close personal relationship. During business hours, the two leaders discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade, and artificial intelligence.In his own toast, Xi noted that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."He said, "These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing." FOLLOW LIVE UPDATES5 Takeaways From the Trump-Xi SummitPhoto Credit: AFPTradeThe United States and China announced the extension of their trade truce as Trump landed in the US, but only a short one. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides agreed to extend by two months a trade agreement that ended last year's trade war and was due to expire in November. The extension would give Washington and Beijing "more time to see what we can do on the economic front," he said.The extension appears to push the central questions surrounding the trade, including tariffs, Chinese purchases, rare-earth supplies, and technology restrictions, into the next round of negotiations.Bessent said that Beijing was meeting its requirement in the earlier agreement to buy 25 million tons of soybeans but was lagging on its pledge to buy $17 billion in other agricultural goods. US officials have said rare-earth deliveries were also falling short, another sign that significant gaps remain.TaiwanThe Chinese leader also pressed Trump on the Taiwan issue, saying Beijing hoped Washington would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence," China's official news agency reported.The agency's English-language service also wrote that Xi hoped the US would oppose Taiwan independence.There are no signs that the Trump administration plans to change Washington's long-standing formulation that it does not "support" independence.So far, the White House has not issued any readout of the exchange, but US officials have long avoided explicitly stating opposition to Taiwanese independence.AIPhoto Credit: AFPThe two leaders expressed diverging views about artificial intelligence. Trump, who has declared that AI should be called super intelligence, or SI, said in a social media post that he wants to "leave it exactly where it is" and rely on the US Department of Justice rather than impose any new guardrails. He insisted that China held the same position.But Xi said that, as leading nations on AI, China and the US must manage their growth. "We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people," he said.Strategic RiskXi once again reiterated his warning that the US and China must avoid the "Thucydides trap," referring to the idea that when a rising power threatens to displace an established one, the result is often war. The Chinese leader had offered a similar warning when Trump visited Beijing in May."It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses," Xi added, arguing that both nations stand to gain from cooperation and lose from confrontation.The Chinese leader insisted the risk "can be overcome," but his reference underscored how concerns about a potential US-China military conflict continue to shadow relations between the world's two largest powers. Xi also called for regular military dialogue and stronger crisis-prevention mechanisms.Trump, for his part, drew on the two nations' shared history to emphasize the potential for cooperation. They could accomplish much by pursuing common interests, he said, invoking their wartime alliance against Japan.Image MakeoverTrump treated Xi's visit as an opportunity to show off a Washington being remade in his image. After Xi treated Trump in Beijing to a tour around a Ming dynasty temple and a walled-off garden retreat rarely opened to foreigners, the US president returned the favor with a different kind of spectacle that included troops wearing wigs and tri-corner hats marching in formation and playing music in a Rose Garden redesigned to look like a Trump golf club.Fighter jets and bombers also roared overhead during ceremonies, one so loud it caused Trump to flinch.The media covering the event wasn't allowed to hear what the two leaders talked about the weighty affairs of state. Instead, it was to watch them tour the Marine One helicopter and the recently redesigned South Lawn of the White House, replete with a large helipad emblazoned with the presidential seal.Speaking to reporters, Trump brushed away questions about their policy discussions. "He loves good granite...Great meeting," Trump said of Xi.
news.summary: The US leader has done his best to impress Xi, praising their close personal relationship. During business hours, the two leaders discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade, and artificial intelligence.

news.title: Trump’s Home County Halts Data Centers Amid President’s AI Push
news.text: Palm Beach County commissioners voted unanimously Thursday to halt new applications for large-scale data centers for up to one year, as the Trump administration pushes to expand the infrastructure needed to support artificial intelligence (AI). The 6-0 vote in Palm Beach County—home to President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate—comes after months of opposition to a proposed expansion of Project Tango, a planned hyperscale AI data center near Arden in western Palm Beach County. The site is about 20 miles west of Trump’s residence and near homes and an elementary school. Several residents addressed the board Thursday, raising concerns about water, higher power bills, environmental impacts and disruptive noise. Thursday’s vote prohibits the county from accepting, processing or approving new applications for data centers in unincorporated Palm Beach County with an anticipated peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts. It does not undo Project Tango’s earlier approval. In July, commissioners rejected a proposal to dramatically expand the development, but a 2016 approval for two 100,000-square-foot data center buildings remains in place. Newsweek reached out to Project Tango for comment. The moratorium gives the county time to develop new rules governing projects that could place significant demands on local power, water and other infrastructure. Trump has pushed back on similar measures, criticizing New York’s decision in July to impose a one-year moratorium on new large-scale data centers. At the time, Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul cited concerns about rising electricity demand, utility costs, environmental impacts and pressure on local communities. Trump called the decision “terrible,” saying data centers are one of the biggest driving forces for jobs in the future. In late August, Trump pushed back on local opposition to data center projects, writing on Truth Social that municipalities rejecting data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor.” “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he wrote. A new Pew Research Center survey found Americans’ views of data centers have shifted more negative since the beginning of the year. More than half of Americans, 54 percent, said data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39 percent in January. Half said they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38 percent, while 49 percent said they are mostly bad for nearby residents' quality of life, up from 30 percent. The survey was conducted from July 20 to August 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Palm Beach County joins a growing number of Florida local governments that have moved to restrict or pause large-scale data center development, including Bay, Citrus, Clay, Holmes, Jackson, Leon, Nassau, Pasco and Walton Counties, according to the South Florida Sun Sentinel. County commissioners also directed staff to explore hiring an outside consultant to help review the rules, after rejecting a proposed technical advisory committee. Vice Mayor Marci Woodward said Thursday she feared the advisory committee would “add an extra layer of work.” Mayor Sara Baxter said she supported the idea of hiring a consultant but objected to the potential cost, which she said could range from about $200,000 to $2 million. The higher figure, Baxter said, was “not even a topic of conversation.” No consultant contract or spending was approved Thursday. The moratorium is set to expire September 24, 2027, or earlier if the county completes its development regulations. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The move follows months of local opposition to a proposed major data center in western Palm Beach County.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Iran offers Trump deal before US elections
news.text:
Iran has offered the US a new deal aimed at ending the months-long conflict before the November midterm elections, directly challenging President Donald Trump’s claim that Tehran is deliberately waiting until after the vote to reach an agreement.

Trump claimed in his UN speech on Tuesday that Iran was deliberately stalling the talks to see how Republicans performed in the November 3 elections and predicted that Tehran would make a deal “right after” the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if negotiations failed.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” he added, referring to a memorandum of understanding reached by Washington and Tehran in June.

“We did reach an agreement with your president… The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, descended into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway,” Pezeshkian added in an interview with Fox News. “We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war… It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has now submitted a proposal under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within about a week and negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program rapidly resumed. The proposal was transmitted to Washington through mediators during talks in New York this week.

Under the plan, Tehran would restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also seeking an end to hostilities on other fronts, including Israel’s combat operations in Lebanon.

US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased arrangement in which the blockade and restrictions on Hormuz would be addressed first, Reuters reported, citing Iranian, regional and Western diplomatic sources.

Tehran has not abandoned its claim to regulate Hormuz, with Iranian officials continuing to insist that the waterway should be managed by Iran and Oman and that fees may be charged for services provided to passing vessels.

Araghchi said the proposal largely follows the terms of the June memorandum rather than introducing new demands. He said Iran was waiting for Washington’s response.

Araghchi has also held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts in New York, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Moscow stressed that there was “no alternative” to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the “illegal actions” of the US and Israel.

The renewed diplomatic push comes amid mounting pressure on both sides. The US blockade has sharply restricted Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran’s controls over Hormuz have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors and helped push oil prices above $100 a barrel and US diesel prices to historic highs.

Pezeshkian, who became the first foreign head of state to speak at the UN while his country was at war with the US, told the chamber on Wednesday that Tehran remained prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but would not negotiate under threats of force and “will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

news.title: Ignored, mocked, harangued – what’s the point of the UN any more?
news.text:
To be sure, Guterres has faced immense challenges. His tenure has seen the highest number of conflicts since the end of World War II, including a major return of interstate conflicts such as Russia’s war against Ukraine, the US and Israel’s war against Iran and clashes between Thailand and Cambodia.

While expansionist leaders such as Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have trampled over the rules-based international order, Guterres has also had to respond to threats including climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic and, now, artificial intelligence. And he’s had to do it with slashed resources thanks largely to Trump’s antipathy to the UN and the “globalist” philosophy it embodies. At the start of his second term, Trump froze almost all US funding for UN humanitarian work and refused to pay into the organisation’s core budget. As a result, the UN has had to lay off 2900 staff, nearly a fifth of its workforce, and embark on a radical reform program, even as it tries to plug gaps left by Trump’s devastating cuts to American aid programs. Staff at key agencies have been shifted en masse from Geneva to Nairobi to save money.

Even so, Cogan says Guterres bears responsibility for “a crisis of morale and of confidence” that he says has beset the UN during his tenure. He accuses Guterres of practising “church mouse diplomacy” with a lack of focus on universal human rights. Like many, he accuses him of soft-pedalling criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic minorities such as the Uyghurs. “Most people I speak to use the word placeholder,” he says. “I don’t see a legacy. I know that’s damning, but it’s the truth.”

Susan Harris Rimmer, an expert in international law at Griffith University, is more complimentary. “He’s had a rough trot, but he’s been exemplary,” she says. “I think he has cut through and been a voice of reason.
